title: Consensus: Raft, Paxos, quorums, split brain
scopeHtml: Scope: Quorums, split brain, Raft election and replication step by step, safety, reads, membership, Paxos intuition, production failure modes. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: What consensus solves
notes.html:
Consensus is getting several machines to agree on one value (or one ordered log of values), even when some machines crash and messages are delayed. Everything that needs "exactly one leader", "this config is the truth", or "this transaction order is final" ultimately rests on it.

Properties required:

  • Agreement: no two nodes decide different values.
  • Validity: the decided value was proposed by someone.
  • Termination (liveness): a decision is eventually reached if enough nodes work and the network is eventually stable.

The FLP result (1985) proves that in a fully asynchronous network no deterministic algorithm can guarantee all three if even one node may crash. Real algorithms (Raft, Paxos) keep safety always and give up guaranteed liveness: during network chaos they may stall, but they never decide wrongly.

Industry examples. etcd (Kubernetes' brain) uses Raft; ZooKeeper uses ZAB; Google Chubby and Spanner use Paxos; Consul uses Raft; CockroachDB runs one Raft group per data range; Kafka KRaft replaced ZooKeeper with a Raft-based controller quorum.

Everyday analogy. A committee deciding the meeting date by phone; some members may be unreachable, but once a majority agrees, the date is fixed and nobody can later claim a different one.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying consensus is needed for everything. Many systems (Dynamo-style, CRDTs) avoid it for availability.
  • Not knowing that consensus sacrifices availability on the minority side of a partition (CAP).

notes.title: Quorums and why majority
notes.html:
A quorum is the minimum number of nodes that must agree for a decision to count. A majority quorum is more than half: floor(N/2) + 1.

Why majority works: any two majorities of the same group share at least one node. So a newer decision must overlap the previous one and will learn about it. That overlap is the whole safety argument.

Cluster size N Majority Failures tolerated
3 2 1
4 3 1
5 3 2
7 4 3

Even sizes add cost but no fault tolerance (4 tolerates the same 1 as 3), so use odd sizes: 3 or 5. More nodes means slower writes (more acks) and more network chatter. etcd recommends 3 or 5 and warns that large clusters get slower.

Read/write quorums (Dynamo style): with N replicas, write quorum W and read quorum R, R + W > N guarantees reads overlap the latest write. N=3, W=2, R=2 is common. This is tunable quorum, different from strict consensus.

Worked example. A 5-node etcd cluster across 3 zones (2,2,1). Losing a whole zone of 2 leaves 3 up = still a quorum. Losing the zone with 2 plus one more node from another leaves 2 of 5 = no quorum, writes stop (reads may also stop for linearizable ones).

Decision gravity. Cluster size is reversible with membership changes (done carefully, one node at a time). Spreading across zones/regions is a latency decision: cross-region quorum adds the inter-region RTT (50 to 150 ms) to every write.

Everyday analogy. A jury needing 7 of 12: any two groups of 7 must share a juror, so two contradictory verdicts cannot both be "official".

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing 4 nodes "for more safety".
  • Putting a 3-node cluster in 2 zones: losing the zone with 2 nodes kills quorum. Use 3 zones.
  • Mixing up consensus quorums with R + W > N tunable quorums.

notes.title: Split brain
notes.html:
Split brain is when two parts of the system each believe they are the leader and both accept writes, so the data diverges. It usually follows a network partition or a long pause on the old leader.

How it happens: network splits 5 nodes into {A,B} and {C,D,E}. A naive "elect a new leader if the old one is silent" rule lets {C,D,E} elect C while A keeps thinking it is leader. Two leaders, two histories.

Prevention:

  1. Majority rule: only the side with a quorum (3 of 5) may elect a leader and commit. {A,B} cannot make progress.
  2. Terms / epochs: every leadership has an increasing number. Messages from an older term are rejected.
  3. Fencing: protect the resource itself so a zombie leader's writes are refused (see the locks notes).
  4. STONITH (shoot the other node in the head): in classic HA clusters, power off the other node via a management interface before taking over.

Real incident pattern. GitHub's 2018 incident: a 43-second network partition between datacenters made the MySQL orchestrator promote a replica on the other coast while writes had already hit the old primary. Divergent data took about 24 hours to reconcile. Symptom: two primaries reporting read_only=OFF; metric: replication errors and conflicting row versions.

Decision gravity. Choosing strict majority consensus (CP) over "always available" (AP) is a one-way product decision: you decide that the minority side refuses writes. Alternatives: multi-leader with conflict resolution (CRDTs, LWW), accepting merge pain.

Everyday analogy. Two team captains each told "you are in charge" by different managers while the phone line was cut; both give orders and the project forks.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing 2 nodes can be made safe with a heartbeat. Two nodes have no majority; add a witness (3rd node/arbiter).
  • Forgetting the paused-old-leader case (GC pause), not only network partitions.

notes.title: Raft overview: roles and terms
notes.html:
Raft makes consensus understandable by splitting it into: leader election, log replication and safety. Every node is in one of three roles.

  • Follower: passive, replies to leader and candidates.
  • Candidate: a follower that timed out and is asking for votes.
  • Leader: the only one that accepts client writes and replicates them.

Time is divided into terms, numbered 1,2,3... Each term has at most one leader. A node that sees a higher term immediately steps down to follower. Terms act as a logical clock for leadership.

Key persistent state on each node (must survive restarts, stored to disk before replying): currentTerm, votedFor, and the log[] of entries, each tagged with its term.

Typical config (etcd defaults, confirm for your version): heartbeat interval 100 ms, election timeout 1000 ms. Election timeout is randomised per node (e.g. 150 to 300 ms in the Raft paper) so that not everyone becomes a candidate at once.

Industry examples. etcd, Consul, TiKV (one Raft group per region), CockroachDB (per range), RabbitMQ quorum queues, Kafka KRaft controller.

Everyday analogy. A classroom: one student is class monitor (leader) for a term; if the monitor goes silent, someone raises a hand to be elected; a new term number starts every election.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking clients can write to any node. Writes go through the leader (followers redirect).
  • Forgetting that currentTerm and votedFor must be persisted before responding.

notes.title: Raft leader election step by step
notes.html:
A follower that hears nothing from a leader for one election timeout becomes a candidate and asks for votes.

Steps:

  1. Follower times out (random 150 to 300 ms, say). It increments currentTerm (term 4 -> 5), votes for itself, becomes candidate.
  2. It sends RequestVote(term=5, lastLogIndex, lastLogTerm) to all peers.
  3. A peer grants its vote if: the candidate's term >= its own, it has not voted in this term, AND the candidate's log is at least as up-to-date as its own (compare last log term first, then last log index).
  4. With a majority of votes, the candidate becomes leader and immediately sends heartbeats (empty AppendEntries) to assert authority.
  5. If votes split (no majority), the timeout expires again with fresh random delays; a new term starts.

Worked example. 5 nodes, leader N1 dies at term 4. N2 (timeout 180 ms) and N5 (timeout 210 ms) time out. N2 starts first, gets votes from N3 and N4 (and itself) = 3 of 5, becomes leader in term 5 before N5's timer fires. Total unavailability about 180 ms plus a round trip. With a 1000 ms election timeout it would be about 1 to 2 s.

Why the log check. It guarantees a leader always has all committed entries ("leader completeness"). A node missing committed data cannot win.

Real incident pattern. Too short an election timeout vs network latency or GC pauses causes constant elections: etcd logs "leader changed" repeatedly, etcd_server_leader_changes_seen_total climbs, writes time out. Fix: raise timeouts, fix disk latency (etcd fsync > 10 ms is a classic cause).

Decision gravity. Election timeout is a reversible tuning knob: shorter means faster failover but more false elections. Rule of thumb: 10x the heartbeat and at least a few multiples of network RTT.

Everyday analogy. The silence in a meeting after the chair leaves: whoever speaks first with a good claim and gets most hands raised becomes chair.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the node with the highest ID wins (that is Bully algorithm, not Raft).
  • Forgetting randomised timeouts exist to avoid split votes.
  • Not mentioning the up-to-date-log restriction.

notes.title: Raft log replication and commit
notes.html:
The leader appends each client command to its log, copies it to followers, and marks it committed once a majority has stored it.

Steps:

  1. Client sends command to the leader.
  2. Leader appends (term, index, command) to its local log (and fsyncs).
  3. Leader sends AppendEntries(term, prevLogIndex, prevLogTerm, entries[], leaderCommit) to followers.
  4. A follower checks that its entry at prevLogIndex has term prevLogTerm. If yes it appends and acks; if no it rejects (log mismatch).
  5. When a majority (including the leader) have the entry, the leader advances commitIndex, applies the entry to its state machine and replies to the client.
  6. Followers learn the new leaderCommit in the next AppendEntries and apply too.

On rejection the leader decrements nextIndex for that follower and retries until logs match, then overwrites the follower's conflicting suffix. This is the Log Matching Property: if two logs have an entry with the same index and term, all earlier entries are identical.

Worked example. 3 nodes, fsync 2 ms, same-zone RTT 0.5 ms. Leader fsync 2 ms in parallel with follower round trip (0.5 ms + follower fsync 2 ms), so commit takes about 3 ms. Throughput is limited by disk fsync: batching 100 entries per fsync gives tens of thousands of writes/s. Cross-region with 80 ms RTT: every write costs at least about 80 ms.

Safety rule. A leader only commits entries from its own current term by counting replicas; older-term entries become committed indirectly once a current-term entry above them commits. (This avoids the Figure 8 anomaly in the Raft paper.)

Industry examples. etcd serves Kubernetes state; its write p99 is dominated by disk fsync, which is why etcd needs SSDs. TiKV batches and pipelines Raft messages for throughput.

Decision gravity. Synchronous majority replication is a one-way semantic choice: durability and linearizability at the cost of latency. Async replication (Postgres default) is faster but can lose acknowledged writes on failover.

Everyday analogy. A secretary reads out a decision; it becomes official only after most committee members write it in their own minutes.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the leader waits for ALL followers. A majority is enough; slow followers catch up later.
  • Confusing "appended" with "committed" with "applied".
  • Forgetting that the leader fsyncs before counting its own vote.

notes.title: Raft safety, reads, and membership
notes.html:
Safety guarantee: once an entry is committed, every future leader has it. It follows from majority overlap plus the vote restriction on log up-to-dateness.

Linearizable reads. A leader may be stale (deposed but unaware). Options:

  • Log read: put the read through the log (slow, always correct).
  • ReadIndex: leader notes commitIndex, confirms it is still leader via a heartbeat round to a majority, waits for apply, then reads. etcd uses this by default for linearizable reads.
  • Leader lease: leader trusts time-bounded lease; faster but depends on bounded clock drift.
  • Follower/stale reads: fast, may be old. etcd offers serializable reads for this.

Membership changes. Changing from 3 to 5 nodes at once could create two disjoint majorities. Raft uses either joint consensus (old+new quorums both required during transition) or single-server changes (add or remove one at a time, safe). etcd adds learners (non-voting) first so a new node catches up before it can affect quorum.

Log growth. Logs are compacted with snapshots; a far-behind follower receives InstallSnapshot. etcd snapshots and compacts by revision; unbounded history hits the DB size quota (default 2 GB, confirm for your version) and the cluster goes read-only with "no space".

Everyday analogy. Before the chair announces "the current decision is X", they quickly check with the room that they are still chair.

Common interview traps.

  • Reading from the leader without confirming leadership and calling it linearizable.
  • Adding two voters at once to a 3-node cluster without learner or joint consensus care.
  • Never compacting etcd.

notes.title: Paxos intuition
notes.html:
Paxos is the original consensus algorithm; Raft is essentially a more structured way to build the same guarantee. Single-decree (basic) Paxos agrees on one value using two phases and three roles (proposer, acceptor, learner; one node often plays all).

  • Phase 1 (prepare/promise): proposer picks a unique, increasing number n and sends Prepare(n) to acceptors. An acceptor that has not promised a higher number replies Promise(n) plus the highest-numbered value it already accepted (if any), and promises to ignore proposals below n.
  • Phase 2 (accept/accepted): if the proposer got promises from a majority, it sends Accept(n, v), where v is the value from the highest-numbered accepted proposal reported (the proposer MUST adopt it), or its own value if none. Acceptors accept unless they promised a higher number.
  • The value is chosen when a majority accepted it.

Why it is safe. The rule "adopt the highest already-accepted value" ensures that once a value could have been chosen by a majority, every later proposal will rediscover it through majority overlap.

Liveness problem. Two proposers can keep preempting each other with higher numbers (dueling proposers). Fix: elect a distinguished proposer (leader), which is exactly what Multi-Paxos does: after phase 1 once, the leader runs only phase 2 for each log slot. That is functionally Raft's leader-based replication.

Industry examples. Google Chubby, Spanner (Multi-Paxos per tablet), Apache Cassandra lightweight transactions (Paxos for compare-and-set), Microsoft Azure storage. Raft was designed (Ongaro and Ousterhout) mainly because Paxos was hard to implement correctly.

Decision gravity. Choosing Raft over Paxos for a new system is a pragmatic, mostly reversible library choice; you rarely write either yourself. Use etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul instead of implementing consensus.

Everyday analogy. Bidding rounds with numbered tickets: if anyone already got a "yes" for some value in an earlier round, the next bidder must carry that value forward instead of pushing their own.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing Paxos as "just majority vote". The adopt-highest-accepted rule is the crux.
  • Not knowing Multi-Paxos is what real systems run.
  • Believing you should implement your own consensus.

notes.title: Raft vs Paxos vs ZAB vs others
notes.html:
Raft Multi-Paxos ZAB (ZooKeeper) Viewstamped Replication
Leader Strong, required Distinguished proposer Strong Primary
Log gaps Not allowed (contiguous) Allowed in theory Ordered by zxid Contiguous
Understandability Designed for it Notoriously hard Medium Medium
Used by etcd, Consul, TiKV Spanner, Chubby ZooKeeper Research, some systems

Related but different: Byzantine fault tolerant protocols (PBFT, Tendermint) handle malicious nodes and need 3f+1 nodes to tolerate f faults; crash-fault protocols like Raft need 2f+1. Use BFT only when nodes may lie (blockchains), not inside your own datacenter.

Leaderless alternatives: EPaxos (no single leader, helps wide-area latency), and Dynamo-style quorum systems with weaker guarantees.

Decision gravity. Choosing a managed coordination service (etcd/ZooKeeper) rather than embedding Raft in your application is nearly always right; embedding is a heavy, hard-to-reverse commitment (you own snapshots, membership, upgrades).

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing Byzantine fault tolerance for an internal service.
  • Saying ZooKeeper uses Raft (it uses ZAB).

notes.title: Consensus performance and failure modes in production
notes.html:
Latency and throughput:

  • Write latency is one disk fsync on a majority plus one network round trip. Cross-AZ adds about 1 ms; cross-region adds the inter-region RTT.
  • Throughput is raised by batching entries, pipelining AppendEntries, and sharding: many small Raft groups (CockroachDB ranges, TiKV regions) each with its own leader spread over nodes.

Typical failure symptoms and metrics:

  • Leader flapping: frequent elections; leader_changes counter rising; cause is disk fsync stalls, network jitter, CPU starvation of the leader process.
  • No quorum: writes fail with timeouts; has_leader=0. Cause is losing a majority or a bad zone layout.
  • Slow follower: one lagging node; leader keeps sending, memory grows. Cause is slow disk or network.
  • Disk full or DB size quota: cluster goes read-only (etcd alarm NOSPACE).

Worked example. etcd with SSD: fsync p99 under 10 ms is the guideline; with a shared HDD fsync can hit 100 ms, heartbeats get delayed beyond the 1 s election timeout and leadership churns, taking Kubernetes API writes down.

Everyday analogy. A committee meeting where the chairperson keeps losing their voice: each time, the room has to re-elect and nothing gets decided.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting etcd on shared slow disks or mixing it with noisy neighbours.
  • Scaling a single Raft group by adding nodes instead of sharding groups.
  • Forgetting monitoring: alert on leader changes and fsync latency.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Consensus = agree on a value or ordered log despite crashes; safety always, liveness only when the network is eventually stable (FLP).
  • Majority quorums overlap, so decisions are never lost; use 3 or 5 nodes across 3 failure domains; even sizes add no tolerance.
  • Split brain = two leaders; prevent with majority rule, terms/epochs, fencing, or STONITH. GitHub 2018 is the classic incident.
  • Raft: follower/candidate/leader, terms, randomised election timeouts, up-to-date-log vote rule; commit when a majority stores the entry; ReadIndex for linearizable reads; safe membership changes; snapshots.
  • Paxos: prepare/promise then accept; adopt the highest accepted value; Multi-Paxos adds a leader. Same guarantee as Raft.
  • Crash faults need 2f+1 nodes, Byzantine need 3f+1.
  • In production: use etcd/ZooKeeper/Consul, fast disks, alert on leader changes and fsync latency, shard into many groups for scale.
